answer: An applicant locks a work seat by binding one address to a numbered yarrow bed for four epochs and publishing a wet-lab pigment curve of that bed's first cutting. Attestors then fire a zephyr test: a 90-second, randomly scheduled solvent draft that only a living cutting shifts into the published curve. Beds shared across addresses, copied curves, or dried leftovers fail, so minting extra votes costs a new plot, a new lab curve, and a live response in the test window.
